meeting_header: Date: 2026-05-20 | Start: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 42m | Attendees: Maya Chen, Derek Alvarez, Priya Raman (Redwood); Aisha Khan, Tom Ruiz, Leah Morgan (Polaris Health)
summary: Redwood AE/SE pair demoed org/project key sandbox in the Console and API patterns for rate limiting, quotas, and multi-tenant controls. Customer probed Dedicated vs Hosted, SOC2/KMS requirements, and request-routing fallbacks for latency-sensitive endpoints. Agreed next steps: share pricing, security artifacts, traffic samples, and a short console video. Pilot kickoff planned early June.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Maya from Redwood here, I think we have like 40 minutes, is that still good?
[00:06] Aisha Khan: Yep that works for us, thanks Maya.
[00:09] Derek Alvarez: Hi, Derek here on the SE side, I'll jump in on the console and the API patterns.
[00:14] Tom Ruiz: Tom from DevOps, curious mostly about rate limits and how we can map to our existing API keys.
[00:19] Leah Morgan: Leah from security, I'll flag compliance and KMS questions.
[00:22] Maya Chen: Awesome. Quick agenda: show the org/project key sandbox in Console, sketch routing/priority lanes, demo policy-driven quotas (burst vs steady), and talk about Dedicated vs hosted implications for latency and encryption. Sound good?
[00:33] Aisha Khan: Yes, particularly the mapping of our internal teams to project keys.
[00:36] Derek Alvarez: Okay, I'll share my screen — if you see a brief console recording, you'll notice we keep keys scoped to projects and orgs.
[00:46] [Screen share noise / brief pause]
[00:50] Derek: So here's the Projects page, we create an Org (polaris-health) and underneath you can create project keys for 'clinical-api', 'billing', 'research-proxy'. Each key gets its own quota band and burst policy.
[01:05] Tom: How do you enforce per-key concurrency? We have spikes around midnight ET and don't want billing jobs to wipe out the clinical latency SLA.
[01:14] Derek: Good question. We have two knobs: steady-state quota (tokens/minute) and concurrency lanes. You can attach a priority policy so clinical-api sits in a high-priority lane with reserved throughput. The low-priority lanes get best-effort and can be throttled using leaky-bucket.
[01:29] Leah: Are those throttles visible in logs for an audit? We need to show throttling events in the next vendor assessment.
[01:35] Derek: Yes, the audit logs capture policy hits, rejections, and fallback events. Note the export includes request ID, org, project, policy applied, and decision reason — helpful for compliance.
[01:46] Maya: Small note, the logs can be pushed to your SIEM through our events stream or pulled via API.
[01:52] Aisha: What about KV cache — you mentioned caching earlier — does that change how quotas work?
[01:58] Derek: Cache (we call it K-V cash in some older notes, apologies for the transcript) is per-model session caching. If a request hits the prefix cache, it bypasses heavy token compute which lowers cost and latency; however quota accounting still increments per request unless you enable a cache-credit policy which deducts different units.
[02:18] Tom: For private deployment, is the rate enforcement inside our VPC or does it route to Redwood control plane?
[02:25] Priya Raman: For Private, the enforcement plane runs in your VPC — control plane signals can be optional. For Dedicated (hosted dedicated capacity) policy decisions can be local to the serving cluster and optionally mirrored to your audit logs.
[02:39] Leah: KMS — does Redwood integrate with our HSM or cloud KMS? We cannot have plaintext keys leave our environment.
[02:46] Maya: We support customer-managed keys via AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and HSM integrations. In Private installs we can configure HSM-backed key wrapping so seeds never leave your enclave.
[02:58] Aisha: How does failover work across regions? We have a read-only regional endpoint for clinical queries in Europe, and don't want cross-region fallbacks to hit US instances with different compliance posture.
[03:11] Derek: We have routing policies: prefer-region, home-region-only, and flexible-fallback. You can set per-key routing so clinical-api is home-region-only for EU workload; if that capacity is exhausted you can set an automatic degrade to a redwood-verified smaller model in-region rather than routing out of region.
[03:29] Tom: So we can have model fallback + policy that blocks cross-region routing?
[03:33] Derek: Exactly. You can chain policies: routing -> model variant fallback -> queue.
[03:38] Leah: Any SOC2 artifacts you can share? Encryption at rest, audit retention windows, RBAC controls?
[03:44] Maya: Yes, we'll send the SOC2 report and the security whitepaper. RBAC is in the Console — roles, admin, audit-only, operator roles — and we support SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning.
[03:58] Aisha: Show us a concrete quota rule example — like clinical-api gets 10 rps steady with a 200 request burst per minute?
[04:08] Derek: Sure. In the policy editor, you define steady window tokens-per-minute and burst window. Here's an example policy: steady=600 tokens/min (10 rps equivalent for our token model), burst=2000 tokens over 1 minute with a cooldown window. You can also attach soft-limits that alert before hard rejections.
[04:28] Tom: Is there a simulator to test our traffic pattern?
[04:31] Derek: Yes, in Optimize we have a Traffic Sim tool — you can upload a 7-day sample and simulate policy hits, predicted latency, and cost. We ran a quick sim for similar healthcare traffic patterns and showed how prefix caching and batching reduced token cost by ~25%.
[04:47] Aisha: About batching — clinical queries are low latency, can batching hurt SLA?
[04:52] Derek: Batching trades some latency for cost. We recommend for non-latency-sensitive endpoints (analytics, research) to enable batching. For clinical real-time RPCs, prefer single-request low-latency lanes and KV cache. Optimize can recommend per-endpoint batching configs.
[05:09] Leah: For the pilot, we need to demonstrate that throttling doesn't silently drop requests and that retries surface the right error codes for our orchestrator.
[05:17] Derek: Standard behavior is 429 with policy metadata in headers (x-policy-id, x-retry-after, x-decision). We also have a webhook hook for immediate notifications on policy rejections so your orchestrator can route to fallback.
[05:29] Tom: How granular can we get on routing? Can keys be split by route path inside the same project key?
[05:35] Derek: Two options: create sub-project keys for the route or use route-scoped policies (prefix match). We usually recommend sub-keys for strong billing isolation; use scoped policies for convenience.
[05:46] [Crosstalk — brief interruptions]
[05:52] Maya: Let me jump in — on the commercial side, Dedicated gives you reserved capacity and lower p99 latency guarantees, hosted gives simpler setup and burstability. For privacy-sensitive workloads we typically recommend Private deployment or Dedicated with VPC peering.
[06:07] Aisha: Cost delta, roughly? We need some numbers to assess economics.
[06:11] Maya: Ballpark, Dedicated reserved capacity reduces per-token cost by 30–40% depending on committed hours; Private has an infra + license model. We'll send a side-by-side in the pricing matrix.
[06:22] Leah: SLA and breach handling? We need clear terms for data residency and audit.
[06:27] Maya: We'll include SLA language in the SOW. For data residency in Private installs it's customer-controlled. For Hosted we offer region-locking and data retention controls.
[06:36] Tom: Can we run a short POC with 10k requests/day and validate throttles and logs?
[06:40] Maya: Absolutely — pilot with a project key scoped to your infra. We typically do a two-week pilot to validate policies and collect traffic.
[06:47] [Screen shift — Derek showing policy editor]
[06:50] Derek: Here is the policy editor — JSON and a GUI. You can author a policy like:
[06:58] Derek (cont): { "policyName": "clinical-high", "steadyTokens": 600, "burstTokens": 2000, "priority": "P0", "region": "eu-west-1", "actions": ["reject", "webhookNotify"] }
[07:13] Aisha: Is that directly deployable to the serving fleet?
[07:16] Derek: Yes — when you hit Deploy it propagates to the routing layer with a canary rollout. If errors spike, the console auto-rolls back.
[07:25] Leah: About canary and rollbacks — how long is the canary window and can we tie it to synthetic evals?
[07:31] Derek: Canary window is configurable; we often use a 10–15 minute window. You can tie it to eval hooks — if quality degrades the rollout stops.
[07:39] Maya: This is part of our quality-first rollout story — avoids deploying a model variant that regresses.
[07:44] Tom: The Customer uses Kong gateway — any reference integration?
[07:48] Priya: We have a Kong plugin template and an Envoy filter example that injects x-org/x-project headers and handles token mapping. We'll share the repo link.
[07:57] Aisha: Could we see a quick API call for enforcing quota? Example request/response?
[08:02] Derek: Sure. Example: POST /v1/response with header Authorization: Bearer <project-key>; response includes x-policy-id and x-remaining-tokens. If rejected, 429 with x-retry-after.
[08:15] Tom: Does the SDK expose token accounting metrics?
[08:19] Derek: Yes — SDK includes counters and a diagnostics endpoint that returns quota usage, token burn, and prefix cache hit rates.
[08:27] Leah: For audit we need immutable logs 90 days — is that standard?
[08:31] Maya: We support configurable retention; hosted default is 30 days, enterprise add-on gives 365 days, Private you control retention.
[08:41] [Pause]
[08:44] Aisha: Can you show the Optimize recommendation for clinical-api — like quantization or batching suggestions?
[08:50] Derek: Right — in Optimize we run an analysis that recommends quantization for non-telemetry models and suggests a cache policy. For clinical-api, the recommendation was: keep int8 quantization off for lowest latency, enable prefix caching, and set batching to disabled. For research-proxy, enable int8 and 128-token batching.
[09:09] Tom: Does quantization affect compatibility with function calling or tool integrations?
[09:13] Derek: Some structured output paths are sensitive; Optimize flags these as 'do not quantize' when it detects function call reliance.
[09:20] Leah: For our internal audit, we want a demo run with sample data sanitized to show logs and webhook notifications.
[09:27] Maya: Yes, we can run a sanitized demo. Derek will produce a console recording and we'll coordinate with Aisha on sanitized traffic.
[09:35] Aisha: Timeline wise, we want pilot in early June and a review with legal in mid-June.
[09:40] Maya: Sounds doable. We'll follow up with dates.
[09:44] Tom: One quick ask — can you simulate degradation and show how fallback to a smaller model affects token economics?
[09:51] Derek: I can run a quick sim: if clinical-api falls back to a 3B in-region variant, p99 latency increases marginally but cost drops ~50%. We'll include simulation numbers in the Optimize report.
[10:06] [Wrap-up chatter, confirmations of next steps]
[10:12] Maya: Recap: We'll send pricing and SOC2; Derek will share console recording and optimize sim; Aisha will send traffic samples; pilot kickoff targeted for first week of June.
[10:24] Aisha: Great, thanks everyone.
[10:27] Leah: Thanks.
[10:29] Maya: Thanks all — we'll follow up.
[10:32] [Meeting ends — informal small talk for a few seconds]
notes: Customer strongly prioritized region-only routing for clinical workloads
They requested 90-day immutable audit logs for initial assessment (enterprise retentions discussed)
Pilot plan: 2-week scoped pilot, send sanitized traffic and console recording
